674.t: Drummers, Ray Anderson's classical students and an eighth-grade pianist
674.s: They discuss drummers and written licks, Ray Anderson's improvisation group and a student who clung to the music.
674.q: Yeah and if you nail something, great. You know like sometimes it’s like that’s — now you might have a great drummer that does that. But don’t try to synthesize that and put it on the drum part and say every drummer has to do that now.

674.t: Taking the music away from big bands
674.s: He throws music on the floor in workshops to show the limits of reading from paper.
674.q: I love going around doing this. I mean when I did that one in Chicago, the kids, first of all the teachers always say like — well I always ask them what they want to do. 396.t: Teaching a gifted student and the boy she harmed with beginner lessons
396.s: She describes a student with natural improvising instincts she is reluctant to correct and an earlier child pianist she held back, and her two other students.
396.q: Yeah, you don’t know what your role is, I know. Well I have three students right now who are super interesting, and one is exactly like that. 576.s: She tells students they can be jazz singers without scatting, prescribes bebop lines as the cure, and says to learn the original melody first.

576.s: She sends pitch problems to voice teachers, teaches students gently, and shows how to count intros, endings and keys using charts copied by Cameron Brown.
576.q: Well… I say go to a voice teacher. I‟m not a voice teacher, you know. 652.t: Teaching people to play what they hear: singing exercise
652.s: Singing with a microphone then playing, his planned demonstration at Western Kentucky University and the Anyone Can Improvise idea.
652.q: Yes there is and I think starting off with the simple scales, one or two like the Dorian minor scale is one of the best places to do — also I ask some students to sing with a microphone and then play. Sing — play. Any more, I just have to use myself as an example because I think all the pros have…

322.t: Teaching as language and lesson one from Joe Allard
322.s: He would like to teach, stresses the space between the notes, and gives Allard's chromatic interval exercise as lesson one.
322.q: Well see I — at this late stage in my life I’d like to teach. But see like people in academia avoid me like the plague. You know? 530.t: Skills for today's students; learning from mistakes in elementary band
530.s: Students should write and score; Jordan lets children's scale mistakes lead to Lydian sounds.
530.q: Oh yeah, definitely. I think they need to know how to write, they need to know how to write scores, they need to get into all of it. And it’s easy enough ‘cause they got all the computers, like the computers have made a whole lot of people composers. I mean people can sit down and compose and…

809.t: Jamey Aebersold camps and letting students create
809.s: Everyone can improvise; he taught for Aebersold and at Skidmore.
809.q: Well I think they can. I was talking about that — I watched a beautiful documentary this morning called “Moonlight Sonata” and it was all about a deaf child who got cochlear implants when he was young, and he got to hear, and he ended up performing. 608.t: Teaching tone, melody and old standards; bridging with people
608.s: His tips for full sound, using old tunes like Jada, and his melodic approach that helped bridging in Blood, Sweat & Tears with Halligan and Kooper.
608.q: And I’m happy. I said — and then if they’re playing a little soft I say, “Look,” I play my horn, I said, “This is what a professional volume is.” I’m not bragging. And I fill up the room. 1003.t: Teaching improvisation to young students with two notes
1003.s: Children are innately creative; Mondello eases fear by giving a student two notes and building up without theory.
1003.q: Very, very good point. I see that and have seen that in my years teaching. I’ve always felt that younger students have an innate creative ability to, what we would call improvise, in many different ways. You see that in art work, you see that in their speaking. The thing about offering jazz improv…

415.t: Teaching in schools and improvising by intuition
415.s: School clinics, forgetting what you know when improvising, and Dizzy's half-step remark.
415.q: Yes. I enjoy that. I like teaching and I enjoy being around students. I’m not self taught as a player though, I studied classical quite a bit. So I’ve had — in fact when I practice now it’s mostly that still. And when I go to these schools, one thing I try to bring to the kids is you can’t forget…

812.t: Amateur singers sitting in and her father's advice; people asking to play her piano
812.s: She recalls her father's coaching about keys and vibrato, and says passers-by sometimes ask to play her piano or doubt she is paid.
812.q: My father all those years ago, when I was like eight and nine or twelve, “Don’t be” you know, “Don’t be like all those people who —” and he just did exactly what you said.

948.t: What a singer must know to work with instrumentalists
948.s: Knowing the melody, counting off, tempo, endings and changes; schools should teach living the music.
948.q: Well you have to be a musician. You have to know how to communicate with the instrumentalists, you have to know how to count off, you have to speak in the language of the musician. Not say, well just know how to talk about the structure of a tune and know what you want, and being able to direct…

671.t: Teaching and the gift of improvisation
671.s: He believes improvisation cannot be taught; students copy him, and he knows the chord changes; he took piano lessons first.
671.q: Yeah. That’s a God given gift. You can tell somebody, write a solo and play it, but you can’t teach people to improvise.

228.t: Ear versus paper, and giving students a concept
228.s: McLean is 98% an ear musician; he develops students' concept by playing them the records that first woke him, from Lester Young to Eckstine, Monk, Dameron and Bird.
